title: Locks, Mutex and atomics
summary: A lock lets only one thread into a piece of code at a time. Use `Mutex` for tiny synchronous sections, actors for async code, atomics for simple counters and flags.
body: **In simple words:** A lock is a key to a room. Only the thread holding the key can enter; others wait outside. It protects shared data in non-async code.

**Choosing:** caller is synchronous and the work is tiny → `Mutex` (iOS 18+, Synchronization module) or `OSAllocatedUnfairLock`. Caller is async or the work may suspend → actor. Just a counter or flag → `Atomic<Int>`.
**Rules:** keep the locked section tiny, never `await` while holding a lock (the compiler blocks this for `Mutex`), and do not call unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock.
**Why not spin locks?** On iOS, spinning wastes CPU and causes priority inversion. `OSSpinLock` was deprecated for this reason.
**Older options:** `NSLock`, `NSRecursiveLock`, serial `DispatchQueue`, `pthread_mutex`. Still valid in legacy code.
keyPoints: `Mutex` for small sync critical sections, actor for async, `Atomic` for counters/flags.
Never hold a lock across `await` or while calling external callbacks.
Unfair locks/Mutex donate priority to the owner; semaphores do not.
`os_unfair_lock` must not be stored as a plain Swift `var`; use `OSAllocatedUnfairLock` or `Mutex`.

code.caption: Mutex and Atomic

mistakes: Doing network or disk work while holding a lock.
Taking two locks in different orders in different places (deadlock).
followups: **Actor or Mutex for an in-memory cache read from many places?** If callers are synchronous and reads are quick, `Mutex`; if fetching may be async, actor.
